source.title: Drawing Multiple Augmentation Samples Per Image During Training Efficiently Decreases Test Error
source.authors: Stanislav Fort; Andrew Brock; Razvan Pascanu; Soham De; Samuel L. Smith

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether averaging gradients across dropout masks changes test accuracy, a different method for examining the dropout generalization effect named in V6.
record.gate_note: The main experiments on augmentation multiplicity, batch sizes, and ImageNet accuracy do not directly test the listed versions. Appendix D reports a Wide-ResNet dropout experiment on CIFAR-100; the dropout-versus-no-dropout comparison is shown in Figure 5(a), and averaging across dropout masks is reported in text and Figure 12.
record.test_reason: Appendix D directly compares dropout with no dropout, testing V6. The batch-size and augmentation-multiplicity experiments also bear on V5's recipe-dependent large-batch penalty and mitigation.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases Appendix D: dropout improves this Wide-ResNet's test accuracy, requires larger epoch budgets, and appears to benefit primarily from its change in the expected gradient rather than mask-sampling variance. The paper's main conclusion is that augmentation multiplicity improves generalization in both small- and large-batch training, including under matched compute budgets, by suppressing detrimental augmentation variance.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines gradient averaging across dropout masks rather than the original version's broader dropout comparisons across fully connected and convolutional classifiers and training-set regimes.
record.method_sensitivity: Dropout-mask averaging did not substantially change test accuracy; the experiment used a 16-4 Wide-ResNet on CIFAR-100 with drop probability 0.4.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging gradients over more dropout masks does not substantially improve test accuracy, despite faster training-loss minimization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this Wide-ResNet, the dropout benefit appears primarily attributable to its change in the expected gradient rather than variance from mask sampling.

record.problems: Dropout comparisons are presented in figures without numeric values in the text; the paper reports no uncertainty for the Appendix D dropout results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps beyond the width needed to interpolate.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning procedures.
Language models, a systematic batch-size threshold, and mitigation through warmup, learning-rate scaling, or normalization changes.
Fully connected classifiers, very small training sets, excessive dropout, and jointly removing dropout and weight decay under augmentation. The tested Wide-ResNet is a convolutional classifier.
Magnitude-aware sharpness as a predictor of generalization gaps; using SAM does not test that correlation.
Removing memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: Matched-epoch small-versus-large batch comparisons: CIFAR-100 batches 64 versus 1024 and ImageNet batches 256 versus 4096, separating conventional augmentation from increased augmentation multiplicity. These curves bear directly on the fixed-epoch batch penalty and its recipe dependence; exact differences need figure inspection.

ImageNet mitigation comparison: at batch 4096, multiplicity 1 peaks at 77.3% after 512 epochs, while multiplicity 8 reaches 78.6% after 128 epochs. Conventional batch-256 training peaks at 77.9% after 512 epochs. Record the conditions and budgets separately rather than treating these peak values as a matched-epoch comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the proposed V6 limits_scope verdict based on R2: V6 does not require mask-sampling variance to explain dropout's benefit. No listed original source is this study. Numerical dropout effects and uncertainties cannot be established from the supplied figure text.

versions.untested_parts: Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Large-batch penalties under fixed epoch budgets and their mitigation.
Very small training sets, convolutional classifiers, and removing dropout together with weight decay under data augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: 16-4 Wide-ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Trained with dropout on the final linear layer; compared with an equivalent network trained without dropout.
rows.locator: Appendix D; Figure 12(a); comparison referenced to Figure 5(a)
rows.note: The text states that networks trained with dropout achieve higher test accuracy than the equivalent network without dropout; numerical values are not given in the text.
rows.check: The dropout benefit is explicitly stated in Appendix D, comparing Figure 12(a) with the no-dropout network in Figure 5(a). Add batch size 64 and note that dropout requires larger epoch budgets; this is not an improvement at every matched training budget. Exact accuracy differences cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.

rows.subject: 16-4 Wide-ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Averaged each gradient over n samples of the dropout mask.
rows.baseline: dropout training with one sampled mask per gradient evaluation
rows.note: Authors state that reducing dropout variance by averaging across multiple masks does not appear to substantially enhance test accuracy.
rows.check: This comparison varies mask averaging while retaining dropout throughout. Its negligible incremental accuracy benefit does not measure dropout versus no dropout, so it cannot establish absence or a scope limitation of V6.

rows.subject: 16-4 Wide-ResNet
rows.operation_detail: Averaged each gradient over n samples of the dropout mask.
rows.note: Figure caption says large numbers of mask samples minimize training loss more quickly; no numerical values are stated.
rows.check: Training-loss convergence under mask averaging does not measure any listed version's held-out generalization effect. The caption explicitly reports faster training-loss minimization with more mask samples, although numerical values are unavailable.

relationships.condition: 16-4 Wide-ResNet on CIFAR-100, final-layer dropout probability 0.4, batch size 64, augmentation multiplicity 1, with sufficiently large training budgets.
relationships.reason: Appendix D explicitly reports higher test accuracy with dropout than without, while requiring larger epoch budgets (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Dropout increased test accuracy but required more training epochs; numerical accuracy gains were unavailable.

relationships.condition: NF-ResNet-50 on ImageNet: large-batch training with augmentation multiplicity versus conventional small-batch training.
relationships.reason: From text, with rows missing: batch 4096 and multiplicity 8 reaches 78.6% at 128 epochs, exceeding the 77.9% peak of conventional batch-256 training across the tested budgets; changing the augmentation recipe can overcome the large-batch penalty.
relationships.display_finding: Using multiple augmented versions of each example (augmentation multiplicity) reportedly gave higher accuracy than conventional smaller-batch training. The comparison remains unverified, and each reported epoch involved more gradient evaluations.

tranche.reason: The dropout-mask averaging and augmentation-multiplicity experiments use different methods to examine dropout generalization and recipe-dependent batch-size effects.

source_check.notes: Dropout accuracy values are figure-only; the textual improvement and larger epoch requirement are explicit. The V5 comparison lacks an extracted row; the paper's epoch definition entails more gradient evaluations as augmentation multiplicity increases.

statements.correction: Section 3/Figure 4(c): NF-ResNet-50, ImageNet, batch 4096, augmentation multiplicity 8, 78.6% top-1 after 128 epochs. Section 2/Figure 3(a): batch 256, multiplicity 1, peak 77.9% after 512 epochs. Supports V5's recipe-adaptation clause.
statements.problem: The numerical comparison is accurate, but classifying this study as evidence against V5 overlooks V5's explicit allowance for recipe changes that remove the large-batch penalty.
